paras: The 1903 Smith County, Mississippi, mob killings and expulsion were an attack by armed white men on a Black settlement near the Smith–Scott county line in early June 1903, in which four or five Black people, one a woman, were killed and eight or ten were beaten. The raid followed the ambush killing of a white man named Craft and the wounding of another, Boyle, which white reports attributed to Black men. The surviving Black residents were ordered out, and lynching lists in both presses counted the dead.

According to the Hattiesburg Daily Progress, a white man it called Croft (elsewhere R. E. Craft) went after a Black laborer who had not finished a paid contract and was waylaid and shot, dying about a week later. Shortly before the raid a second white man, James Boyle (also printed Boyles, Boys and Boyce), was shot from ambush and wounded. The wire stated that both were shot "by negroes," but no report in the coverage describes an arrest or charge for either shooting.

White men of the neighborhood then armed themselves and, in the Hattiesburg paper's words, "began the hunt for negroes like they would for bear." A Globe-Democrat special dated June 8 said four Black people, one a woman, were killed "last night" and two houses burned. A New Orleans dispatch to the New York Sun named two of the dead, William Hornsby, whom it called "the murderer of Craft," and his sister Mary, and said the mob burned the house in which Hornsby had barricaded them and shot them when the flames drove them out. The most widely reprinted version, a Commercial Appeal special from Forest, gave four men and a woman killed, "eight or ten" badly beaten and most other Black residents ordered to leave, by men from Craft's section, which one Memphis report called "the noted Sullivan's Hollow community."
The whites then gave the Black residents three weeks to go, after which, the Hattiesburg paper wrote, those who stayed "would be planted in the ground."

The sheriffs of both counties went to investigate. No report of an arrest, inquest or indictment appears in the coverage. On June 17 a New Orleans dispatch put the Black dead at seven, and the Hattiesburg paper announced peace with the line "P. S.—The negroes are all gone."

The Vicksburg Herald faulted Gov. Longino over "the recent race troubles in Smith," which it called "negro baiting"; the Brookhaven Leader replied that he knew nothing until the main part of the mischief was done. A Jackson tally counted the five as killed "in an uprising against the whites" rather than as lynchings, though June lynching lists included them.

White papers ran the Commercial Appeal account on June 8 and 9 under headlines such as "War on Negroes" and "Negroes Are Driven Out"; the Salt Lake Herald called it a "Tennessee Race War." The wire named none of the dead, and one Memphis version admitted "The names of the dead negroes could not be learned." The Sun headlined "Lynched Four Negroes." The nearby Hattiesburg Daily Progress called it a "Small Race War," said an "organized band" of Black men was believed to be assassinating whites, and titled its editorial on the expulsion "Solving the Problem."

Black papers mostly reprinted: the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate ran the wire as "Kill Five Negroes" and the Western World the Globe-Democrat special. The Western World also printed a correspondent's note from Forest, dated June 6, saying two Black men and a woman were lynched and the rest driven away. The Chicago Broad Ax blamed "a mob of Christians" and stressed that none of the victims had been convicted of any crime. The Savannah Tribune, Indianapolis Freeman and Seattle Republican ran digest items or lynching lists.

The toll was five in the wire and the Broad Ax, four in the Sun and Hattiesburg reports, three in the Western World note, and seven in the latest report, of June 17; the Savannah Tribune alone said two white men had been killed. The scene is put in northern Smith County, southern Scott County, or on their border, and the date as June 6 (the correspondent), the night of June 7 (Globe-Democrat) or Monday, June 8 (digests and lists).

reader.title: 1903 Smith County, Mississippi, mob killings and expulsion
bases: Armed white men raided a Black settlement near the Smith-Scott county line, killed four to five people, beat eight to ten, burned at least two houses and ordered the remaining Black residents to leave (A9, A5, A17).

A 'mob of whites' or band of white men killed at least four Black people without legal process, in retaliation for the ambush shooting of Craft and Boyle that white reports attributed to Black men, and the Sun named one victim as Craft's alleged murderer (A4, A5, A9); contemporary June lynching lists counted the dead (A31, A32).

Independent dispatches (the Commercial Appeal special A9, a Globe-Democrat special A20, a New Orleans dispatch A4), the nearby Hattiesburg paper (A5) and a Black correspondent at Forest (A19) all report Black people killed by whites after the Craft shooting, though they differ on the count.

accounts.label: Commercial Appeal special (wire)
accounts.gist: Four men and a woman killed, eight or ten beaten, the rest ordered to leave after Craft was shot from ambush and Boyle wounded 'by negroes'; done by men from Craft's part of the country.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch to the Sun
accounts.gist: Four killed by a white mob in southern Scott County; Hornsby, called Craft's murderer, and his sister were shot when the mob burned them out of their house.

accounts.label: Globe-Democrat special
accounts.gist: After an attempt on James Boyles late Friday, four Black people including a woman were killed the night before the June 8 dispatch and two houses burned.

accounts.label: Hattiesburg Daily Progress
accounts.gist: Croft was shot after a labor dispute, a second white man waylaid; whites hunted Black people 'like bear', killed four, burned houses and gave the rest three weeks to leave.

accounts.label: Black correspondent at Forest
accounts.gist: Two Black men and a woman were lynched and the other Black residents driven away, in a note dated June 6.

accounts.label: Later New Orleans report
accounts.gist: On June 17 the trouble was over and seven Black people had been killed in all.

framing.detail: The Commercial Appeal wire ran under 'War on Negroes', 'Negroes Are Driven Out', 'Negroes Killed and Survivors Driven Off' and, in Salt Lake, 'Tennessee Race War', stating the shootings were 'by negroes'.
The Sun headlined 'Lynched Four Negroes' but called Hornsby 'the murderer of Craft' without qualification.

The Hattiesburg Daily Progress called it a 'Small Race War', said an 'organized band' of Black men was believed to be assassinating whites, and treated the expulsion as 'Solving the Problem', ending 'The negroes are all gone.'
A Jackson tally called it 'an uprising against the whites' and excluded it from actual lynchings; the Vicksburg Herald, quoted by the Leader, called it 'negro baiting'.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate ran the wire as 'Kill Five Negroes' and the Western World reprinted the Globe-Democrat special.
The Chicago Broad Ax blamed 'a mob of Christians' and said innocent people suffered though none had been convicted; the Western World's correspondent called it lynching.
The Savannah Tribune ran a one-line digest item; the Freeman and Seattle Republican listed the dead among June lynchings.

record_check.dossier: community_attack: a raid on a Black settlement with killings (which meet the lynching definition), beatings, house burning and expulsion
Uncertain, June 6-8: correspondent's 6-6 dateline, Globe-Democrat 'last night' of June 7, most digests and lists Monday June 8
Forest (Forrest) is the dispatch dateline; the killings were in a settlement near the Smith-Scott county line
Smith or Scott: northern Smith (wire), southern Scott (Sun), the border of the two (Hattiesburg)
William Hornsby (Hornby) and his sister Mary; no 'Moes' appears in any article about this event
5 in most reports; 4, 3 and a later 7 also reported
White men from Craft's section, said to be from the 'Sullivan's Hollow community' of southern Smith County; none named
'a mob of Christians' is the Chicago Broad Ax's own ironic phrase, not a white description; the summary should also cite the expulsion

info: Killings reported by June 6 (Western World correspondent), on the night of June 7 (Globe-Democrat special), or Monday June 8 (Savannah Tribune, Greenville Times, lynching lists); wire dispatches dated June 8.
A Black settlement near the line between Smith and Scott counties; dispatches datelined Forest (Forrest), Miss.; 'northern part of Smith county' (wire), 'southern part of Scott county' (Sun).
William Hornsby (Hornby) and his sister Mary named; the other dead unnamed.
Retaliation for the ambush killing of R. E. Craft and wounding of James Boyle, attributed by white reports to Black men; the Sun called Hornsby 'the murderer of Craft'.
White men from Craft's part of the country; a Memphis version says from the 'Sullivan's Hollow community' of southern Smith County.
Five (four men, one woman) in most reports; four including a woman in others; three in the Western World correspondent's note; seven in a June 17 report.
Black residents left the neighborhood; by June 17 'The negroes are all gone.'
